Week 4 · Lecture 4 and Lab 4

IP addresses, and the services that hand them out

Lecture 4 explains what an IP address is, how IPv4 and IPv6 differ, and the different kinds of address. Lab 4 shows the three services every network relies on: DHCP gives out addresses, DNS turns names into addresses, and a web server sends the pages. The rest of the IP lecture (classes, subnetting and NAT) is in Week 5.

Lecture 4

Internet Protocol (IP)

6 Oct
4.1

What is an IP address?

In plain wordsAn IP address works like a postal address. A postal address names the street first, then the house on that street. An IP address does the same: the first part names the network, and the last part names one device on that network.

An Internet Protocol address, or IP address, is a logical address given to every device on a network so that it can communicate.

Logical, not physical
A MAC address is burned into the network card. An IP address is assigned to the device, and it can change.
Hierarchical
It contains network information and host information, in that order.
Unique
Within one network, no two devices can have the same IP address.

An IPv4 address is 32 bits long, split into two parts. The network ID says which network the device is on. The host ID says which device it is on that network.

Where the split falls is set by the subnet mask, which is the main topic of Week 5.

Why do we need IP addresses?

Billions of devices need to communicate. Data has to travel across many networks to get anywhere. And every router on the way needs to know where to send each packet.

Follow one request. Your phone has the address 192.168.1.5 on your home network, and your home router is 192.168.1.1. Facing the Internet, the router has one public address from your ISP, for example 203.0.113.5. The ISP and the backbone routers each have many addresses, and the server at the end has its own.

Check yourself

In your phone's address, 192.168.1.5, which part picks out your phone rather than the network?

In one line: an IP address is a changeable, two-part address, the network first and the device second. Next, the two versions of IP.

4.2

IPv4 and IPv6

In plain wordsThink of car number plates. When a country starts running out of plate numbers, it makes the plates longer. IPv4 addresses are running out, and IPv6 is the much longer plate.

IPv4, Internet Protocol version 4
  • It was created in 1981.
  • It uses 32-bit addresses: 4,294,967,296 possible addresses, about 4.3 billion.
  • It is written in dotted decimal, like 192.168.1.100. Each of the four numbers is one octet (8 bits), from 0 to 255.
IPv6, Internet Protocol version 6
  • It was created in 1998 (RFC 2460).
  • It uses 128-bit addresses: about 340 undecillion (3.4 × 10³⁸).
  • It is written in hexadecimal, in eight groups separated by colons: 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334
FeatureIPv4IPv6
Address size32-bit128-bit
FormatDotted decimalHexadecimal
Total addresses~4.3 billion~340 undecillion
Header size20–60 bytes40 bytes (fixed)
NATCommonly usedNot needed
SecurityOptional (IPSec)Built-in (IPSec)
ConfigurationManual / DHCPAuto-configuration (SLAAC)
BroadcastYesNo (uses multicast)
Check yourself

How long is an IPv6 address?

In one line: IPv4 is 32 bits in dotted decimal and is running out; IPv6 is 128 bits in hexadecimal. Next, how a device gets its address.

4.3

Static and dynamic addresses

In plain wordsA dynamic address is like a hotel room: you are given one when you arrive, and next time it might be a different room. A static address is like your home address: it never changes, so people always know where to find you.

Dynamic IP address
  • It is assigned automatically by DHCP, and it can change over time.
  • It is used for client devices and home networks.
  • Pros: it is easy, it avoids conflicts, and it uses addresses efficiently.
  • Cons: the address can change.
Static IP address
  • It is configured by hand, and it never changes.
  • It is used for servers, printers, routers and IoT devices.
  • Pros: it is predictable and easy to manage.
  • Cons: it has to be set up by hand, and two devices could be given the same address by mistake.

Servers, printers and routers get static addresses because other devices have to find them at the same address every time. In Lab 4 the server is given the static address 192.168.1.2, while the PCs get theirs from DHCP.

Check yourself

The office printer receives jobs from every computer. Should it have a static or a dynamic address?

In one line: dynamic addresses come from DHCP and can change; static ones are set by hand and stay put. Next, the four ways an address can be used to send.

4.4

Unicast, broadcast, multicast and anycast

In plain wordsThink of talking. Whispering to one friend is unicast. Shouting to the whole room is broadcast. Posting in a group chat that only members see is multicast. Calling a pizza chain's single number and getting the nearest branch is anycast.

Unicast
One to one. It is the most common type, used for web browsing and email.
Broadcast
One to everyone on the network (IPv4 only). Used by ARP requests and DHCP discovery. Address: 255.255.255.255 (limited broadcast) or the subnet's broadcast address.
Multicast
One to many: only devices that joined the group. Used for streaming and video conferencing. Range: 224.0.0.0 – 239.255.255.255.
Anycast
One to the nearest. Several servers share one address, and your traffic reaches the closest one. DNS root servers and content delivery networks, CDNs, use it.
Check yourself

A new laptop sends a DHCP Discover to every device on the LAN. Which type is that?

In one line: unicast to one, broadcast to all, multicast to a group, anycast to the nearest. Next, Lab 4: the services that hand out addresses.

Lab 4

Network services: DHCP, DNS and web servers

Packet Tracer
4.5

Three network services

In plain wordsMoving into a new flat needs three helpers. Someone gives you your address and keys. A phone book lets you find people by name. And the shops hand over what you ask for. In a network those are DHCP, DNS and a web server.

Network services are functions provided by devices on a network so that computers can communicate and exchange information.

Picture a company where staff need to connect their computers to the network, reach websites by name, and open a website hosted on an internal server.

ServiceMain jobExample
DHCPAssigns IP configuration automaticallyPC gets 192.168.1.10
DNSTurns domain names into IP addresseswww.example.com → 93.184.216.34
Web serverStores and delivers web contentA PC opens a website

The lab asks: what would happen if every computer needed someone to set its IP address by hand? Every machine would need a visit, mistakes would creep in, and two computers could end up with the same address.

Keep them apartThese are three separate services. A web server does not give out addresses or answer DNS questions, even when all three run on the same physical machine.

Check yourself

Which service turns www.example.com into an IP address?

In one line: DHCP gives you an address, DNS finds addresses by name, and the web server sends the content. Next, DHCP in detail.

4.6

DHCP: getting an address automatically

In plain wordsDHCP is like checking into a hotel. You ask reception if there is a room. They offer you room 10. You say yes, room 10 please. They confirm and hand you the key. The key only works until checkout, and that time limit is the lease.

DHCP, the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol, automatically gives devices the IP configuration they need to communicate.

It can provide an IP address, a subnet mask, a default gateway, and a DNS server address, plus how long the device may keep them.

Why do we need it?

Imagine 100 computers with no DHCP. Someone would have to type the IP address, mask, gateway and DNS server into every one.

  • That is a lot of manual configuration.
  • Two devices might be given the same address by mistake, which is an IP conflict.
  • Changing a setting later means visiting every device again.
  • And it does not scale to hundreds or thousands of devices.

The DHCP client is the device asking for a configuration, like a laptop, a phone or a printer. The DHCP server hands it out. That can be a dedicated server, a router with DHCP turned on, or a server running DHCP software.

How DHCP works: DORA
  1. Discover: the client broadcasts a message to find a DHCP server. It has no usable IP address yet.
  2. Offer: a DHCP server replies with an offer: a proposed IP address and settings.
  3. Request: the client replies that it wants to use the offered configuration.
  4. Acknowledge: the server confirms with a DHCP ACK, and the client sets itself up with those settings.
Address pool and lease

The address pool is the range the server may hand out. Example: network 192.168.1.0/24, pool 192.168.1.10 – 192.168.1.100.

The lease is how long a client may use its address, for example 24 hours. Before it runs out, the client normally tries to renew it.

Why leases? Think of a university where students join the Wi-Fi for a few hours. Leases let those addresses go back into the pool instead of being kept forever for every device that ever connected.

Check yourself

What is the order of the four DHCP messages?

In one line: DHCP hands out an address, mask, gateway and DNS server in four steps, D O R A, for a limited lease. Next, DNS.

4.7

DNS: from names to addresses

In plain wordsDNS is the contacts list of the Internet. You tap a name, and your phone dials the number saved under it. You type a website's name, and DNS finds the IP address saved under it.

DNS, the Domain Name System, translates domain names into IP addresses, so that clients can find services by name instead of remembering numbers.

Compare 192.168.1.3 with www.company.local. Staff will find the name much easier to remember, and DNS stores the link between the two.

RememberDNS only finds the address. It does not host the website or send the pages.

How a name gets resolved
  1. You type www.company.local, and the computer needs its IP address.
  2. The client sends a DNS query to its DNS resolver, asking for the address of www.company.local.
  3. The DNS server replies: www.company.local → 192.168.1.3.
  4. The client contacts the web server at that IP address.
  5. If the web service is running and the connection works, the browser shows the website.
DNS records

DNS stores its information in records. Each record type has a job.

RecordPurposeExample
AName → IPv4 addresswww.company.local → 192.168.1.3
AAAAName → IPv6 addressa domain → an IPv6 address
CNAMEAlias for another nameshop.company.com → store.company.com
MXMail servers for a domaincompany.com → mail server
NSAuthoritative name serversa domain → its name server

In the lab you only need the A record: name www.example.com, type A, address 192.168.1.2.

The lab asks: what if the record pointed to the wrong IP address? The browser would contact the wrong machine, so the site would fail to load or the wrong site would appear.

Check yourself

Which record maps a name to an IPv6 address?

In one line: DNS looks a name up and returns its IP address, using records like A, AAAA, CNAME, MX and NS. Next, the web server.

4.8

Web servers and HTTP

In plain wordsA web server is like a restaurant kitchen. DNS tells you where the restaurant is. You place your order, which is the HTTP request. The kitchen sends out the dish, which is the HTTP response.

A web server is a system that hosts web content and delivers it to clients. It can be a physical computer, a virtual machine, a cloud system, or just a service running on a computer.

It talks to web browsers using HTTP or HTTPS.

What happens when you open a website
  1. You type http://www.company.local.
  2. The browser asks DNS for the address, and gets back 192.168.1.3.
  3. The browser connects to the server on TCP port 80 for HTTP, or port 443 for HTTPS.
  4. It sends an HTTP request, for example asking for the main page.
  5. The web server sends an HTTP response containing HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images or other content.
  6. The browser draws the page, and you see the website.
The request
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.company.local
The response
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
Status codeMeaning
200 OKRequest succeeded
301 Moved PermanentlyPermanent redirect
403 ForbiddenServer refuses access
404 Not FoundResource not found
500 Internal Server ErrorThe server hit an error
TechnologyPurpose
HTTPTransfers web content
HTTPSHTTP protected by TLS
HTMLStructure of the page
CSSHow it looks
JavaScriptBehaviour in the browser

RememberDNS finds the server's IP address. HTTP or HTTPS carries the conversation. The web server answers with the content.

Check yourself

The browser shows 404. What does it mean?

In one line: the browser finds the server with DNS, asks with an HTTP request on port 80 or 443, and the server answers with a status code and the page. Next, building all three in Packet Tracer.

4.9

The Packet Tracer lab

In plain wordsPicture one building with three separate counters inside: one hands out addresses, one is the phone book, and one serves web pages. In the lab, one Server-PT runs all three services, but each counter does its own job.

The network
DeviceIP addressJob
Router192.168.1.1Default gateway
Switch—Connects the LAN
Server-PT192.168.1.2DHCP + DNS + HTTP
PC0, PC1from DHCPClients
Option A: everything on the server
  1. Server static settings (Desktop → IP Configuration): IP 192.168.1.2, mask 255.255.255.0, gateway 192.168.1.1, DNS 192.168.1.2.
  2. Services → DHCP → On. Pool LAN_POOL: gateway 192.168.1.1, DNS 192.168.1.2, start 192.168.1.10, mask 255.255.255.0, maximum users 50.
  3. Services → DNS → On. Add an A record: www.example.com → 192.168.1.2 (the same server hosts the site, so it points to itself).
  4. Services, HTTP: turn it on, and edit index.html to show a message such as Welcome to our Networking Lab.
  5. On each PC, set IP Configuration to DHCP, then open the web browser and go to http://www.example.com.

Three things happen. DHCP gives the PC its configuration. DNS tells the PC which address belongs to www.example.com. HTTP fetches the page from that address.

Option B: DHCP on the router

The router can run DHCP too. It stays the default gateway, and now it also hands out the addresses.

Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/0
Router(config-if)# ip address 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.0
Router(config-if)# no shutdown
Router(config-if)# exit
Router(config)# ip dhcp excluded-address 192.168.1.1 192.168.1.9
Router(config)# ip dhcp pool LAN_POOL
Router(dhcp-config)# network 192.168.1.0 255.255.255.0
Router(dhcp-config)# default-router 192.168.1.1
Router(dhcp-config)# dns-server 192.168.1.2
Router(dhcp-config)# lease 7
Router(dhcp-config)# exit
Router(config)# end
Router# copy running-config startup-config
  1. enable, then configure terminal, gets you into configuration mode.
  2. The interface commands give the port facing the switch its address, 192.168.1.1, and no shutdown switches it on.
  3. ip dhcp excluded-address 192.168.1.1 192.168.1.9 reserves .1 to .9, so DHCP never gives away the router's or the server's address.
  4. ip dhcp pool LAN_POOL creates the pool. network says which addresses to give out, default-router gives clients their gateway, and dns-server tells them to use the Server-PT for DNS.
  5. lease 7 makes each address last 7 days.
  6. copy running-config startup-config saves the setup so it survives a restart.
CommandLease length
lease 77 days
lease 11 day
lease 0 1212 hours
lease 0 0 3030 minutes
lease infiniteNever expires

Then turn DHCP off on the Server-PT, so the router is the only DHCP server on the LAN. The server keeps running DNS and HTTP. The router only tells clients which DNS server to use.

This works because everything is on one subnet. If you add another subnet later, the router needs DHCP relay, so clients there can reach the DHCP server.

Test it

On PC0, choose DHCP and check it gets an address such as 192.168.1.10, mask 255.255.255.0, gateway 192.168.1.1 and DNS server 192.168.1.2. In the command prompt, run ipconfig, then ping 192.168.1.1 to test the router and ping 192.168.1.2 to test the server. Finally, open http://www.example.com in the browser.

Router or server?DHCP is a service, not a kind of hardware, so either can run it. In a small network the router is enough. A larger network often uses a dedicated server, for central management and flexibility.

Check yourself

What does ip dhcp excluded-address 192.168.1.1 192.168.1.9 do?

In one line: one Server-PT can run DHCP, DNS and HTTP, or the router can take over DHCP; either way, test with ipconfig, ping and the browser. Next week: classes, subnetting and NAT.

Extra

Extra lectures: the tricky parts, one at a time

optional
E4.1

DHCP: checking into a hotel

You arrive at a hotel with no room. You do not even know who works at reception, so you call out to the whole lobby: is there a room for me?

DiscoverThat shout to everyone is the Discover. It is a broadcast, because you have no address yet and do not know the server's address.

OfferReception answers: you can have room 10. That is the Offer.

RequestYou reply: yes, I will take room 10. That is the Request.

AcknowledgeReception confirms and gives you the key, plus the Wi-Fi password and the restaurant's location. That is the Acknowledge, carrying your address, mask, gateway and DNS server.

Your key stops working at checkout. That is the lease. Stay longer, and you renew at the desk before it runs out.

Your turn

Which DHCP message is sent as a broadcast, because the client has no address yet?

In the storyIn the network
shouting to the lobbyDiscover (broadcast)
you can have room 10Offer
I'll take room 10Request

checkout timethe lease
E4.2

One trip to a website, all three services

Follow a brand new PC, from switching on to seeing a web page.

1 · DHCPThe PC has no address. It runs DORA and gets 192.168.1.10, the mask, the gateway, and the DNS server, 192.168.1.2.

2 · DNSYou type www.example.com. The PC asks the DNS server at 192.168.1.2, and the A record answers: 192.168.1.2.

3 · HTTPThe browser connects to 192.168.1.2 on port 80 and sends GET. The web server answers 200 OK with the page.

If DHCP fails, the PC has no address and nothing works. If DNS fails, you can still reach the site by typing its IP address. If the web service is off, the name resolves but the page never loads.

Your turn

Typing 192.168.1.2 opens the site, but www.example.com does not. Which service is broken?

Week 5 · Lecture 5

Classes, subnetting and NAT

Lecture 5 finishes the Internet Protocol: the old address classes, why CIDR replaced them, subnet masks, how to find a network's range and split it into subnets, DHCP and APIPA, public and private addresses, and NAT. Subnetting questions are calculations, so this week starts with the binary you need for them.

Lecture 5

Internet Protocol (continued)

17 Oct
5.1

Octets and binary: the tool you need first

In plain wordsAn octet is a row of eight light switches. Each switch is worth a fixed amount: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1. Switch some on and add up their values, and you get any number from 0 to 255.

This lesson is not a slide of its own, but the subnetting slides use it on every line, so learn it first.

An IPv4 address is 32 bits, written as four octets of 8 bits each. That is why each number in an address goes from 0 to 255.

Bit1st2nd3rd4th5th6th7th8th
Value1286432168421

The values halve from left to right: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. All eight on is 255. All off is 0.

192 = 128 + 64, so the first two are on: 11000000.

In a subnet mask, the ones always come first, then the zeros. So a mask octet can only take these values.

Ones from the leftBinaryValue
110000000128
211000000192
311100000224
411110000240
511111000248
611111100252
711111110254
811111111255

One more rule. With n bits you can count 2 to the power n different values. 2 bits give 4, 6 bits give 64, and 8 bits give 256.

Check yourself

A mask octet is 11100000. What number is that?

In one line: an octet is eight bits worth 128 down to 1, and n bits give 2 to the power n values. Next, the old address classes.

5.2

IP classes, A to E

In plain wordsImagine a T-shirt shop that only sells three sizes: enormous, medium and small. Classful addressing was like that. A network came in just three sizes, A, B or C, and the first number of the address told you which.

Classful addressing was used on the early Internet, from 1981 to 1993. Network sizes were fixed by class, and the first octet decided the class.

ClassFirst octetFirst bitsDefault maskNetworksHosts per network
A1 – 1260255.0.0.0 (/8)126 (2⁷ − 2)16,777,214 (2²⁴ − 2)
B128 – 19110255.255.0.0 (/16)16,384 (2¹⁴)65,534 (2¹⁶ − 2)
C192 – 223110255.255.255.0 (/24)2,097,152 (2²¹)254 (2⁸ − 2)
D224 – 2391110Multicast
E240 – 2551111Experimental

Class A was for large organisations, ISPs and governments. Class B was for medium to large organisations. Class C was for small organisations and home networks.

Slide examples: 10.0.0.1 (A) → network 10.0.0.0. 172.16.0.1 (B) → network 172.16.0.0. 192.168.1.1 (C) → network 192.168.1.0. The host part is the rest: 0.0.0.1.

Gap at 127127 is missing from the table because it is reserved for loopback: 127.0.0.1 always means this computer itself.

Check yourself

Which class is 150.10.20.30?

In one line: the first octet gives the class, and the class fixes the network size. Next, why that failed, and CIDR.

5.3

Why classes failed, and CIDR

In plain wordsBack to the T-shirt shop. A company with 300 staff is too big for a class C, with 254 hosts, so it gets a class B with 65,534, and wastes over 65,000 addresses. CIDR lets the shop cut any size it likes.

Problems with classful addressing
Wasteful allocation
Class A had 16 million hosts, too many for most. Class C had 254, too few for many. There was no middle ground.
Routing table explosion
Millions of class C networks meant enormous routing tables.
Inflexibility
There were no custom sizes, so organisations were stuck with a fixed class.
Rapid exhaustion
Class B addresses ran out first, in the 1990s.

The solution was CIDR, Classless Inter-Domain Routing.

CIDR was introduced in 1993, in RFC 1519, and replaced classful addressing. It allows variable-length subnet masks, called VLSM, so a network can be any size.

CIDR writes the size after a slash: 192.168.1.0/24. The number after the slash is the prefix length, the number of network bits.

  • /24 = 24 network bits, 8 host bits
  • /16 = 16 network bits, 16 host bits
  • /30 = 30 network bits, 2 host bits

The ruleHost bits = 32 minus the prefix. CIDR has no classes, so any prefix length is valid.

Check yourself

In 10.0.0.0/20, how many host bits are there?

In one line: classes wasted addresses, so CIDR lets the prefix after the slash set any size. Next, turning a prefix into a mask and a host count.

5.4

Subnet masks and how many hosts

In plain wordsA subnet mask is a stencil laid over the address. Where the stencil has ones, that part is the network and is fixed. Where it has zeros, the space is open for host numbers.

A subnet mask is 32 bits: ones for the network bits, then zeros for the host bits. /26 = 26 ones then 6 zeros = 255.255.255.192.

  1. Host bits equal 32 minus the prefix.
  2. Total addresses equal 2 to the power of the host bits.
  3. Usable hosts equal that total minus 2.

Why minus 2?The first address in every network is the network address, the name of the network itself. The last one is the broadcast address, which reaches every host. Neither can be given to a device.

CIDRSubnet maskHost bitsTotalUsable
/8255.0.0.02416,777,21616,777,214
/16255.255.0.01665,53665,534
/24255.255.255.08256254
/25255.255.255.1287128126
/26255.255.255.19266462
/27255.255.255.22453230
/28255.255.255.24041614
/29255.255.255.248386
/30255.255.255.252242
/31255.255.255.254122
/32255.255.255.255011

The last two are special cases. A slash 31 is used for a link between just two routers, so no network or broadcast address is set aside. A slash 32 is one single host.

ShortcutEach step down the table halves the addresses: 256, 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4. Remember those and you can rebuild the whole table.

Check yourself

How many usable hosts are in a /27?

In one line: host bits are 32 minus the prefix, there are 2 to the power host bits addresses, and you take 2 off for the network and broadcast. Next, finding exactly which addresses those are.

5.5

Network address, broadcast and host range

In plain wordsA network is a row of numbered seats. The first seat is the row's name plate, so nobody sits there. The last seat holds the loudspeaker for the whole row. Everyone else sits in between.

Lecture example: 192.168.1.0/26 
IP:   192.168.1.0  = 11000000.10101000.00000001.00|000000
Mask: /26          = 11111111.11111111.11111111.11|000000
                                     network bits | host bits
  1. Network address: set every host bit to 0. That gives 192.168.1.0.
  2. Broadcast address: set every host bit to 1. The last octet becomes 0 0 1 1 1 1 1 1, which is 63, so the broadcast is 192.168.1.63.
  3. First usable address: the network address plus one, 192.168.1.1.
  4. Last usable address: the broadcast minus one, 192.168.1.62.
  5. Usable hosts: 2 to the power 6, minus 2, which is 62.

The quick wayBlock size = 256 minus the interesting octet of the mask. For slash 26 that is 256 minus 192, which is 64. Networks start at multiples of 64: 0, 64, 128, 192. Each broadcast is one less than the next network.

Try the quick way: 192.168.1.100/26
  1. Block size: 256 minus 192 is 64.
  2. Which block holds 100? The blocks start at 0, 64, 128 and 192. 100 is between 64 and 128, so the network is 192.168.1.64.
  3. The next block starts at 128, so the broadcast is 192.168.1.127.
  4. The usable hosts run from 192.168.1.65 to 192.168.1.126.
Check yourself

Which network does 192.168.1.200/26 belong to?

In one line: host bits all zero give the network, all one give the broadcast, and the hosts sit in between. Next, splitting a network into subnets.

5.6

Subnetting, step by step

In plain wordsSubnetting is cutting a cake into equal slices. You can only cut in halves, then halves again, so you get 2, 4, 8 or 16 slices. To make the slices, you borrow bits from the host part and give them to the network part.

Lecture example: 192.168.1.0/24, we need 4 subnets
  1. Step 1, bits needed. 4 subnets is 2 to the power 2, so borrow 2 bits. The new prefix is 24 plus 2, which is slash 26.
  2. Step 2, subnet size. Host bits are 32 minus 26, which is 6. Hosts per subnet are 2 to the power 6, minus 2, which is 62.
  3. Step 3, the increment. The mask's last octet is now 192, and 256 minus 192 is 64. So the subnets go up in steps of 64.
  4. Step 4, list them.
SubnetNetworkFirst hostLast hostBroadcast
1192.168.1.0/26.1.62.63
2192.168.1.64/26.65.126.127
3192.168.1.128/26.129.190.191
4192.168.1.192/26.193.254.255
Borrowed bits and mask values
Bits borrowedBinaryMask octetSubnets
000000000—1
110000000.1282
211000000.1924
311100000.2248
411110000.24016
511111000.24832
611111100.25264
711111110.254128

Not a power of two?Round up. If you need 5 subnets, 2 bits only give 4, so borrow 3 bits and get 8. You can leave the spare subnets unused.

Check yourself

You split 192.168.1.0/24 into 8 subnets. What is the new prefix?

In one line: borrow enough bits for the subnets, then host bits, block size, and list them. Next, DHCP again, and what happens when it fails.

5.7

DHCP and APIPA

In plain wordsIf nobody at the hotel reception answers, you cannot just stand in the lobby forever. So you write a temporary name badge for yourself. It lets you chat with other guests who did the same, but you still cannot leave the hotel. That badge is APIPA.

DHCP, the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol, automatically assigns IP addresses to devices, using the four DORA steps: Discover, Offer, Request and Acknowledge.

It provides an IP address, a subnet mask, a default gateway, DNS servers, and a lease duration.

What if DHCP fails?

APIPA, Automatic Private IP Addressing: if no DHCP server answers, the device gives itself an address from 169.254.0.0 – 169.254.255.255.

With that address it can only talk to other APIPA devices, not the router and not the Internet.

Read it as a warningA 169.254 address in ipconfig means something is wrong: the DHCP server is down or unreachable, or the cable is unplugged.

Check yourself

ipconfig shows 169.254.33.7. What does that tell you?

In one line: DHCP gives the settings, and a 169.254 address means it failed. Next, public and private addresses.

5.8

Public and private addresses

In plain wordsA company has one public phone number that anyone in the world can call. Inside, every desk has an extension, like 101 or 102. Thousands of other companies use the same extension numbers, and that is fine, because extensions only work inside the building.

The public IP address

A public address is globally unique and can be routed on the public Internet.

  • It is assigned by ISPs, from blocks given out by IANA and the regional registries.
  • It must be unique worldwide.
  • It can be reached directly from the Internet.
  • It is needed to host a public service, like a website.
The private IP address
  • It can be reused inside every private network.
  • It cannot be routed on the public Internet.
  • It needs NAT to reach the Internet.
  • It saves public IPv4 addresses.
ClassPrivate rangeCIDRAddresses
A10.0.0.0 – 10.255.255.25510.0.0.0/816,777,216
B172.16.0.0 – 172.31.255.255172.16.0.0/121,048,576
C192.168.0.0 – 192.168.255.255192.168.0.0/1665,536

Exam trapThe class B private range stops at 172.31. So 172.20.1.1 is private, but 172.32.1.1 and 172.15.1.1 are public.

Check yourself

Which of these is a private address?

In one line: public addresses are unique worldwide; private ones (10, 172.16 to 31, 192.168) are reused everywhere and need NAT. Next, NAT itself.

5.9

NAT and PAT

In plain wordsA hotel has one outside phone number. When room 12 calls out, the receptionist writes down which line room 12 used. When the answer comes back on that line, she puts it through to room 12. The router does the same with addresses and port numbers.

Network Address Translation, NAT, translates private IP addresses into public ones, and back again, as traffic passes through a router.

IPv4 conservation
Many devices share one public IP address.
Security
Devices inside are hidden from the Internet.
Flexibility
You can change ISP without renumbering the inside network.
Three types of NAT
Static NAT, one to one
A permanent mapping: one private address always uses one public address. It is used for servers that need a fixed public presence.
Dynamic NAT, many to many
The router has a pool of public addresses and lends them out as needed, first come, first served. It is limited by the size of the pool.
PAT, or NAT overload, many to one
The most common type. Many private addresses share one public address, and port numbers tell the connections apart.
How PAT works

Three devices visit the same website, 93.184.216.34:80, all from port 5000: laptop .10, phone .11, tablet .12.

Private IP : portPublic IP : portDestination
192.168.1.10:5000203.0.113.45:4000193.184.216.34:80
192.168.1.11:5000203.0.113.45:4000293.184.216.34:80
192.168.1.12:5000203.0.113.45:4000393.184.216.34:80

All three leave with the same public address, 203.0.113.45, but each gets its own public port. When a reply comes back to port 40002, the router looks up its table and sends it to the phone.

Check yourself

A reply arrives at 203.0.113.45:40003. Which device gets it?

In one line: NAT swaps private addresses for public ones at the router, and PAT lets a whole home share one public address using ports. That is the end of the IP lecture.

Extra

Extra lectures: the tricky parts, one at a time

optional
E5.1

Subnetting: one street, equal blocks

Picture a street with 256 houses, numbered 0 to 255. That is a slash 24.

The council splits it into 4 equal blocks. 256 divided by 4 is 64 houses per block, so the blocks start at 0, 64, 128 and 192.

First houseIn each block, the first house holds the block's sign, the network address. Nobody lives there.

Last houseThe last house holds the block's loudspeaker, the broadcast address. Nobody lives there either.

So in the block from 64 to 127, house 64 is the sign, 127 is the loudspeaker, and people live in 65 to 126. That is 62 homes.

The block size is also 256 minus the mask octet. For 4 blocks the mask octet is 192, and 256 minus 192 is 64. Same answer.

Your turn

The street is split into 8 blocks. House 100 is in a block whose sign is at house…

In the storyIn the network
the street, 256 housesa /24
a blocka subnet
houses per blockblock size, 256 − mask octet
the signnetwork address
the loudspeakerbroadcast address
E5.2

Spot the class and the private range in seconds

Exam questions often just ask: which class is this, and is it private? You only need the first number, and sometimes the second.

ClassUp to 126 is A. 128 to 191 is B. 192 to 223 is C. 224 to 239 is D, multicast. 240 and up is E.

PrivateStarts with 10: private. Starts with 192.168: private. Starts with 172, then 16 to 31: private. Anything else is public.

Special ones: 127 is loopback, this computer. 169.254 is APIPA, meaning DHCP failed.

Try it on 172.30.4.9. 172 is between 128 and 191, so it is class B. The second number, 30, is between 16 and 31, so it is private.

Your turn

What about 200.100.50.25?

E5.3

NAT: the hotel switchboard

A hotel has 100 rooms but only one outside phone number.

Room 12 calls a restaurant. The receptionist puts the call out on line 1, and writes in her book: line 1 is room 12.

Room 30 calls the same restaurant. She uses line 2, and writes: line 2 is room 30.

The restaurant calls back on line 2. She checks her book and puts it through to room 30.

In the networkThe rooms are private addresses. The hotel number is the public address. The line numbers are the public ports, and her book is the NAT translation table.

Nobody outside ever learns the room numbers. That is the security benefit of NAT.

Your turn

In the network, what is the receptionist's book?

Week 6 · Lecture 6

Network security

Lecture 6 covers what security is protecting (the CIA triad), the main kinds of network attack, defence in layers, stateless and stateful firewalls, access control lists with their wildcard masks, and the ways security controls are classified.

Lecture 6

Network Security

Lecture 6
6.1

The CIA triad

In plain wordsThink of a letter you post to the bank. Nobody else should read it: that is confidentiality. Nobody should change the amount on the way: that is integrity. And the bank should actually be open when you need it: that is availability.

Confidentiality, integrity and availability are called the CIA triad. They are the three basic security goals for data and for computer services. The US standard FIPS 199 lists exactly these three as the security objectives.

Confidentiality
Data confidentiality means private information is not shown or given to people who are not allowed to see it. Privacy means people control what information about them is collected, stored, and shared, and with whom.
Integrity
Data integrity means data, stored or travelling in packets, and programs are only changed in an allowed way. It includes authenticity, meaning the data really is what it claims to be, and nonrepudiation, meaning neither the sender nor the receiver can later deny the exchange. System integrity means a system does its job without being tampered with.
Availability
Systems work promptly, and service is not denied to authorised users.

Two more goals are often added.

Authenticity
Being able to verify and trust something: users are who they say they are, and every input comes from a trusted source.
Accountability
A security breach can be traced to the person responsible. Systems keep records of activity, for later forensic analysis or to settle disputes.
Check yourself

A flood of traffic takes the bank's website offline. Which goal is attacked?

In one line: keep it secret, keep it unchanged, keep it working, and know who did what. Next, the attacks against those goals.

6.2

Types of network attacks

In plain wordsA passive attacker is someone quietly listening at your door. An active attacker breaks in, moves things, or blocks the door so nobody can get through.

As businesses rely more on networks, attackers exploit weaknesses to get in without permission, steal information, disrupt services, or damage systems. Targets range from single devices to company networks to parts of the Internet itself.

Passive attacks: eavesdropping and surveillance

The attacker watches traffic without changing it, and secretly collects things like passwords, financial details or private messages.

Example: packet sniffing, using a tool like Wireshark to capture data that is not encrypted.

Active attacks: disruptive and malicious

The attacker changes, disrupts, or injects data. They may alter or destroy data, plant malware, or take control of devices.

DoS and DDoS
Denial of Service floods a network or server with traffic until it stops working. Distributed DoS does it from many machines at once.
Session hijacking
Taking over an active session between two users.
Spoofing
Pretending to be another device to get access.
Malware-based attacks
Ransomware
Encrypts your data and demands payment to unlock it.
Worms and viruses
Malware that copies itself and spreads across networks.
Wireless attacks

Wireless networks are more exposed, because the signal is open to anyone nearby.

Evil twin
A fake Wi-Fi network set up to look real, so it can capture users' data.
Wi-Fi eavesdropping
Listening to unencrypted traffic on public Wi-Fi.
Check yourself

Someone runs Wireshark on a café network and reads unencrypted logins. Passive or active?

In one line: passive attacks listen, active attacks change or block, malware infects, and wireless attacks exploit the open air. Next, how to defend in layers.

6.3

Defence in layers

In plain wordsA castle does not rely on one wall. It has a moat, a wall, guards at the gate, locked doors inside, and lookouts on the towers. If one fails, the next one still stands.

A multi-layered defence stacks several independent controls at different points of the system. The goal is redundancy: if one control fails, the others still stand. The result is that attackers need more effort, money and time, which gives you time to detect them and respond.

The five layers
Perimeter defence
Controls who gets into the network in the first place. Examples: next-generation firewalls, secure web gateways, email security gateways, and DDoS protection.
Identity and access
Makes sure only authorised people and systems reach your assets. Examples: multi-factor authentication, privileged access management, role-based access control, and just-in-time access.
Host and application
Protects the computers and software where data lives. Examples: endpoint detection and response, application allow-listing, and runtime application self-protection.
Data security
Protects the data itself, wherever it is. Examples: encryption at rest, in transit and in use, data loss prevention, and tokenisation or data masking.
Visibility and intelligence
Detects and investigates unusual activity, and responds to it. Examples: SIEM, user and entity behaviour analytics, threat intelligence platforms, and security orchestration, SOAR.
Check yourself

Multi-factor authentication belongs to which layer?

In one line: five layers, from the edge of the network to the data itself, so one failure is never the end. Next, firewalls at the perimeter.

6.4

Stateless and stateful firewalls

In plain wordsA stateless firewall is a guard who checks every visitor against a list, but forgets each one the moment they pass. A stateful firewall is a guard who remembers who went out, so when they come back with a reply, he lets them straight in.

Packet-filtering firewalls come in two basic types, depending on whether they track connections.

Stateless firewall

It examines each packet on its own. It does not remember earlier packets or the state of a connection.

It checks the source IP address, the destination IP address, the source and destination ports, and the protocol, compares them with its rules, and allows or blocks the packet.

Example rule: allow TCP from 192.168.1.0/24 to port 80. Every packet for port 80 is judged by this rule alone, without knowing if it belongs to an existing connection.

  • Advantages: fast, simple, and uses few resources.
  • Disadvantages: it cannot understand the context of a connection, secure rules are harder to write, and some packet-manipulation tricks can fool it.
Stateful firewall

It keeps track of the state of active connections. When a client sends a request to a web server, the firewall records that connection in a state table.

For example, the client sends TCP SYN, the server answers SYN-ACK, and the client sends ACK. The firewall records the connection as ESTABLISHED, so the server's return traffic is allowed because it belongs to that connection.

Source IPSource portDestination IPDest. portProtocolState
192.168.1.105152093.184.216.34443TCPESTABLISHED

When the reply comes back (93.184.216.34:443 → 192.168.1.10:51520), the firewall finds it in the state table: it belongs to an existing connection, so it is allowed. A stateless firewall would just test the reply against its rules, not knowing the client started it.

  • Advantages: more secure than basic filtering, understands connections, lets legitimate replies back in automatically, and suits modern networks.
  • Disadvantages: needs more memory and processing, is more complex, and lots of connections use more resources.
FeatureStatelessStateful
Tracks connectionsNoYes
State tableNoYes
Examines packetsIndividuallyIn context of the connection
PerformanceGenerally fasterSlightly slower
Resource useLowHigher
SecurityBasicStronger
ExampleBasic packet-filtering ACLModern network firewall
Check yourself

Which firewall lets a web server's reply back in because it remembers your request?

In one line: stateless judges each packet alone; stateful remembers connections in a state table. Next, access control lists, the rules themselves.

6.5

Access control lists

In plain wordsAn ACL is the bouncer's list at the door of a club. Each line says who may come in and who may not, and the bouncer reads the list from the top.

An Access Control List, ACL, is a set of rules that routers and firewalls use to decide whether traffic is permitted or denied, based on specific criteria.

An ACL can act as perimeter defence, filtering traffic at the boundary between a trusted network and an untrusted one, like the Internet.

What an ACL can check
  • The source IP address.
  • The destination IP address.
  • The protocol: TCP, UDP or ICMP.
  • The source and destination port.
  • The direction of the traffic, in or out.
Main types of ACL
Standard
Filters mainly by source IP address.
Extended
Filters by source, destination, protocol and port.
Numbered
Identified by a number, which also says whether it is standard or extended.
Named
Identified by a name instead of a number, which is easier to read.

Worth knowingThis is not on the slides, but it is how every Cisco ACL behaves. The router reads the rules from the top and stops at the first one that matches. Anything that matches no rule is denied, because there is an invisible deny all at the end.

Check yourself

You want to block FTP but allow web traffic from the same network. Which type of ACL do you need?

In one line: an ACL is an ordered list of permit and deny rules on addresses, protocols and ports. Next, the wildcard masks that ACLs use.

6.6

Wildcard masks

In plain wordsA wildcard mask is a "must match" stencil. A 0 means this bit has to be exactly the same. A 1 means don't care. It is the opposite way round from a subnet mask.

A wildcard mask tells the router which bits of an IP address must match, and which bits can be anything.

  • 0 means must match.
  • 1 means can be different, so it is ignored.
Slide example: one network

To match 192.168.1.0/24 (subnet mask 255.255.255.0), use the wildcard 0.0.0.255.

The first three octets must match, and the last octet can be any value.

The ruleWildcard mask = 255 minus the subnet mask, one octet at a time.

Subnet mask octetWildcard octet
2550
2541
2523
2487
24015
22431
19263
128127
0255

Example: a /26 has mask 255.255.255.192. 255 − 192 = 63, so its wildcard is 0.0.0.63.

Check yourself

What is the wildcard mask for a /28 network?

In one line: 0 must match, 1 is ignored, and the wildcard is 255 minus the mask. Next, writing standard and extended ACLs.

6.7

Standard and extended ACLs

In plain wordsA standard ACL only asks "where are you from?". An extended ACL also asks "where are you going, and what for?".

Standard ACL
  • It filters mainly on the source IP address.
  • It can permit or deny traffic from one host or a whole network.
  • It gives basic traffic control.
  • It is usually placed close to the destination.
access-list <number> {permit | deny} <source> <wildcard-mask>
access-list 10 permit 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255

This allows traffic from the 192.168.1.0/24 network, and other sources are denied.

Extended ACL
  • It gives more detailed filtering.
  • It can check the source IP, the destination IP, the protocol, and the source and destination ports.
  • So it can control single services, like HTTP, HTTPS, SSH or FTP.
  • For example, it can allow HTTP from a network to a web server but deny FTP.
access-list <number> {permit | deny} <protocol> <source> <source-wildcard> <destination> <destination-wildcard> [operator port]
access-list 100 permit tcp 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 host 192.168.10.10 eq 80
  1. access-list 100: an extended ACL, because 100 is in the extended range.
  2. permit tcp: allow TCP traffic.
  3. 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255: from any device on 192.168.1.0/24.
  4. host 192.168.10.10: to that one web server. "host" means every bit must match.
  5. eq 80: only to port 80, which is HTTP.
ACL number ranges
TypeNumbersFilters on
Standard1–99, 1300–1999Source IP address
Extended100–199, 2000–2699Source, destination, protocol, ports
Check yourself

access-list 150 … is which type of ACL?

In one line: standard checks only the source, extended checks source, destination, protocol and port, and the number tells you which. Next, how security controls are classified.

6.8

Security controls by function

In plain wordsProtecting a house: a lock stops the burglar, an alarm tells you he is there, insurance and a new door fix things afterwards, and a sign saying "CCTV in use" makes him think twice.

Security control taxonomies are structured ways of sorting security controls into categories, so an organisation can protect its network systematically. There are two main ways to sort them: by function, and by nature.

Sorting by function asks one question about any control: what is its main job when dealing with a threat, and when does it act?

Preventive
Stops an incident from happening at all, by blocking unauthorised activity. Examples: firewalls, encryption, and multi-factor authentication. It answers: how do we block this threat? On its own it is brittle, because not every threat can be predicted.
Detective
Assumes some attacks will get through, and spots them as they happen or soon after. Examples: SIEM systems, intrusion detection systems, IDS, and audit logs. It answers: how do we know this is happening?
Corrective
Acts after an incident is detected, to contain the damage, remove the threat and get back to normal. Examples: backups and disaster recovery, patch management, and incident response playbooks. It answers: how do we fix it?
Deterrent
Discourages an attacker before they try, by making the attack look risky or hard. Examples: visible cameras, warning banners at login, publicised prosecutions, and security staff. It answers: how do we make this not worth it?
Check yourself

An intrusion detection system raises an alert. Which kind of control is it?

In one line: prevent, detect, correct, deter. Next, sorting the same controls by what they are made of.

6.9

Security controls by nature

In plain wordsThe same house again. The alarm system is technical. The family rule "last one out locks the door" is administrative. The fence and the lock are physical.

Sorting by nature asks what form a control takes and how it is put in place.

Technical controls
Also called logical controls: technology that enforces security rules automatically. Examples: firewalls, endpoint detection and response agents, identity and access management systems, and encryption. They work without constant human help, but only if they are set up and maintained correctly. A misconfigured one gives a false sense of security, or becomes a weakness itself.
Administrative controls
The policies, procedures, standards and guidelines that set security expectations and responsibilities. They are about people and behaviour. Examples: a security policy, security awareness training, risk assessments, background checks when hiring, and incident response plans.
Physical controls
Real-world barriers and monitoring that protect buildings, server rooms, equipment and people. Examples: badge access and biometric locks, cameras and patrols, locked cabinets for backups, and environmental controls like a UPS and fire suppression.

One control, two labelsThe two sortings work together. A firewall is technical by nature and preventive by function. A security camera is physical, and both detective and deterrent.

Check yourself

Yearly security awareness training for all staff is which kind of control by nature?

In one line: technical, administrative, physical. That is the end of Lecture 6.

Extra

Extra lectures: the tricky parts, one at a time

optional
E6.1

Stateful firewall: the guard with a notebook

An office building has one guard at the door.

Going outSara walks out to buy lunch. The guard writes in his notebook: Sara went out to the café.

Coming backSara returns with her lunch. The guard checks the notebook, sees she went out, and lets her straight in.

A strangerA stranger walks up and says, I am bringing lunch back. There is nothing in the notebook, so the guard turns him away.

The notebook is the state table. A stateless guard has no notebook: he would have to judge Sara and the stranger only by a fixed list of rules, without knowing who actually went out.

Your turn

In the firewall, what is the guard's notebook?

In the storyIn the network
Sara going outyour request leaving
the notebookthe state table
Sara coming backthe server's reply, allowed
the strangerunrequested traffic, blocked
E6.2

Wildcard masks in three quick steps

Exams love asking for the wildcard mask. Here is the fastest way.

Step 1Write the subnet mask. For example, a slash 27 is 255.255.255.224.

Step 2Take each octet away from 255. 255 minus 255 is 0, three times. 255 minus 224 is 31.

Step 3Write it out: 0.0.0.31.

A quick check: the wildcard's last octet is always the block size minus one. A slash 27 has blocks of 32, and 32 minus 1 is 31.

And for a single host, every bit must match, so the wildcard is 0.0.0.0. That is what the word host means in an ACL.

Your turn

What is the wildcard mask for a /25?

E6.3

Which control is it?

Every control gets two labels: what it does, and what it is. Try each one before you read the answer.

A firewallIt blocks traffic before harm is done, so it is preventive. It is technology, so it is technical.

Nightly backupsThey let you restore data after an attack, so they are corrective. They are a technical system.

A login warning bannerIt warns that activity is monitored, to put attackers off, so it is a deterrent. It is shown by a computer, so it is technical.

A badge reader on the server roomIt stops strangers walking in, so it is preventive. It is a real-world barrier, so it is physical.

An incident response planIt guides the team in fixing an incident, so it is corrective. It is a written procedure, so it is administrative.

Your turn

A motion sensor that sets off an alarm in the server room is…

Units practice

In the exam a number without the right unit loses marks. Convert units, pick the right unit for an answer, and catch the unit mistakes students make. When you calculate, you choose the unit yourself. Pick the weeks you have covered so far (Week 3 has no calculations).

The unit rules
  • Bytes → bits: × 8. Bits → bytes: ÷ 8. Capital B is bytes, small b is bits.
  • k = 1,000 · M = 1,000,000 · G = 1,000,000,000. So 5 Mbps = 5,000,000 bps.
  • s → ms: × 1,000. ms → s: ÷ 1,000. μs is a millionth of a second.
  • km → m: × 1,000. The signal speed is in m/s, so distance must be in m.
  • Before L ÷ R: size in bits, rate in bps. The answer is then in seconds.
  • Never add ms to s. Change one so both match first.

Coursework · KH5037CMD

Milestone 1, explained

A plain-words overview of what Milestone 1 asks for. It explains the ideas only: the design, the build and the report have to be your own work. Check Moodle for the official brief, the deadline and the report template.

The coursework at a glance

The coursework is the whole module mark. It has three milestones, and Milestone 1 is worth 20% of it. It is individual work, and you may be asked to explain it in a one-to-one discussion.

The scenario

A company wants a secure network split into zones, such as admin, finance, HR, guests and servers. There is a client network for the staff, a server network for the company's services, a router joining them, and a firewall protecting the servers. You play the network engineer who designs and builds it.

What Milestone 1 asks you to build

You build it in Cisco Packet Tracer, using the devices Packet Tracer supports.

FeatureIn plain words
VLANsSplit one switched network into separate departments that cannot see each other by default.
New for the coursework
SubnettingGive each VLAN its own IP network, sized for how many devices it has.
Week 5: subnetting
Inter-VLAN routingLet the VLANs talk to each other through a router, only where you allow it.
Week 3: layer 3
Firewall with ACLsRules on the router that permit or deny traffic, for example keeping guests away from the servers.
Week 6: network security
STPSpare links between switches for backup, without creating loops.
New for the coursework
EtherChannelBundle two or more cables between switches into one faster link that survives a cable failing.
New for the coursework
Port securityA switch port only accepts the device it expects, and blocks or shuts down if another device is plugged in.
New for the coursework
DHCP snoopingThe switch only trusts DHCP offers from the real server's direction, so a fake DHCP server cannot hand out bad settings.
Week 4: DHCP

What you hand in

  • Your Packet Tracer file (.pkt).
  • A report as a PDF, using the template on Moodle. It must explain your IP addressing table, your VLAN design, your subnetting decisions and your routing method.

What the marking looks for

  • A network that is designed and configured correctly: addressing, routing and connectivity all work.
  • Good use of Packet Tracer and sound technical skills.
  • Testing: evidence that you checked it works, such as pings, traceroutes and show command output, and that you found and fixed problems.
  • Security that is in place and shown working, for example traffic that is blocked when it should be.
  • Clear, well-organised documentation with diagrams and evidence.

Write it yourselfThe brief forbids using AI tools to draft paragraphs or sections of the report, and reports may be checked. It is individual work: designs or wording that look shared can be marked as copied. Use this page to understand the ideas, then make your own design and write your own report.

Review

Cheat sheet

Everything from Weeks 1–6 on one page.

Delays (Lecture 1 & 2)

Tap a formula to see what each letter means.

Transmission delayL / R?

Time to push every bit of one packet onto the link.

L
packet length, in bits (bytes × 8)
R
link rate, in bits per second

ExampleA 1,500-byte packet = 12,000 bits on a 10 Mbps link: 12,000 ÷ 10,000,000 = 0.0012 s = 1.2 ms.

Depends on packet size and link speed, not on distance.

Propagation delayd / s?

Time for one bit to travel the length of the link.

d
length of the link, in metres
s
propagation speed in the medium, about 2 × 10⁸ m/s in copper or fibre

Example1,500 km = 1,500,000 m: 1,500,000 ÷ 200,000,000 = 0.0075 s = 7.5 ms.

Depends on distance, not on packet size.

Nodal delayproc + queue + trans + prop?

The total delay a packet picks up at one router (one hop).

proc
processing: the router checks the packet and picks the output link
queue
queuing: time waiting in the output buffer
trans
transmission delay, L / R
prop
propagation delay, d / s

Example0.5 ms + 2 ms + 1.2 ms + 7.5 ms = 11.2 ms.

Store-and-forward over n linksL/R₁ + L/R₂ + …?

Time for one packet to cross several links, when each router must receive the whole packet before sending it on.

L
packet length, in bits
R₁, R₂, …
the rate of each link, in bits per second

Example12,000 bits over two 1 Mbps links: 0.012 + 0.012 = 0.024 s.

If every link has the same rate R, this is just n × L/R.

TDM: time-division multiplexing

Tap a formula to see what each letter means.

Slot rate (your rate)R ÷ N?

How many bits per second one connection gets. Also called the circuit rate.

R
the link rate: total speed of the whole link, in bits per second
N
number of slots in each frame = number of connections sharing the link

Example1.536 Mbps link, 24 slots: 1,536,000 ÷ 24 = 64,000 bps (64 kbps).

Your turn comes the same number of times per second (the frame rate), however many connections share the link. What changes is how much you send per turn: more connections means shorter slots, fewer bits per turn, and a lower slot rate. Example: 4 connections on 1 Mbps get 250 kbps each; 8 connections get 125 kbps each.

Slot rate, the other wayframe rate × bits per slot?

The same slot rate, worked out from how often your slot comes round.

frame rate
how many frames (full rounds of turns) happen per second
bits per slot
how many bits you send in each of your turns

Example8,000 frames/s × 8 bits = 64,000 bps, the same as 1,536,000 ÷ 24.

Frame rate = how many turns you get per second (never changes). Bits per slot = how much you send each turn (shrinks as more connections join). Slot rate = turns × bits per turn.

Total time to send a filesetup + F ÷ slot rate?

How long a whole file takes over a TDM circuit, from start to finish.

setup
circuit setup time, in seconds (ms ÷ 1,000)
F
file size, in bits
slot rate
your rate, R ÷ N, not the link rate

Example0.5 s + 640,000 ÷ 64,000 = 0.5 + 10 = 10.5 s.

The usual mistakes: dividing by the link rate, or adding 500 ms to 10 s without converting.

FDM and circuit sharing

Tap a formula to see what each letter means.

Circuit sharelink rate ÷ circuits?

The rate each circuit gets when a link is split equally.

link rate
total capacity of the link
circuits
how many circuits share it

Example10 Mbps shared by 10 circuits: 1 Mbps each.

FDM max userstotal ÷ per-user band?

How many users fit when each needs its own band.

total
total bandwidth of the link
per-user band
bandwidth each user needs

Example20 Mbps total, 2 Mbps per user: 20 ÷ 2 = 10 users.

Unused FDM capacity(circuits − active) × per circuit?

Capacity wasted by idle circuits, which stay reserved.

circuits
total circuits on the link
active
circuits actually transmitting
per circuit
rate of one circuit

Example12 circuits of 2 Mbps, 9 active: (12 − 9) × 2 = 6 Mbps unused.

Throughput and packet loss (Lecture 2)

Tap a formula to see what each letter means.

Throughput (bottleneck)min(R₁, R₂, …)?

The fastest rate data can cross a whole path. It is set by the slowest link.

R₁, R₂, …
the rate of each link on the path

ExampleLink A 100 Mbps, link B 10 Mbps: 10 Mbps.

Arrival rateN × r?

How fast data arrives at a router from several senders together.

N
number of sources sending
r
rate of each source

Example5 sources at 2 Mbps each: 10 Mbps arriving.

If this is more than the output link can send, the queue grows.

Packets per secondrate ÷ packet bits?

How many packets a rate carries each second.

rate
bits per second
packet bits
size of one packet in bits (bytes × 8)

Example20 Mbps with 8,000-bit packets: 20,000,000 ÷ 8,000 = 2,500 packets/s.

Packets dropped(sent − forwarded) − queue?

How many packets are lost when a router is overloaded.

sent
packets arriving from the sender
forwarded
packets the output link can send
queue
packets the buffer can hold

Example(2,500 − 1,250) − 100 = 1,150 packets lost.

OC-n (fibre speed levels)n × 51.8 Mbps?

The speed of an Optical Carrier level.

n
the level number, as in OC-3 or OC-48

ExampleOC-3: 3 × 51.8 ≈ 155 Mbps.
